Dual Citizenship and Wicked Problems: A Leadership Stance in Child and Adolescent Psychoanalytic Psychotherapy

Andrew Dawson and Lynda Ellis

Lynda Ellis

UK
andrew.dawson@ggc.scot.nhs.uk

UK

Lynda Ellis   Trained at the Tavistock Clinic and worked for many years as a Consultant and Lead child and adolescent psychotherapist within CAMHS. After taking up a post as a Clinical Director of the Northern School of Child and Adolescent Psychotherapy she became Director of that organisation and worked at a senior leadership level within the NHS Trust. She is a Fellow of the British Psychoanalytical Society and is in private practice as a psychoanalyst. She is involved in a number of developments in the Midlands and Northern Region and in teaching and writing.
Leadership, dual citizenship, psychoanalytic child psychotherapy, service development, Wicked problems, organisational dynamics, clinical leadership

This paper raises and addresses issues to do with leadership and child psychotherapy, beginning with a report on a systematic review of papers about leadership in the Journal of Child Psychotherapy (JCP). The authors establish that leadership is expressed implicitly rather than as an important issue in its own right with relevance to clinical work, service development and the ongoing viability of psychoanalytic child psychotherapy. When reviewing the limited literature available, the authors classify them into five types of article: tribute to leaders past; clinical leadership; threat to survival and call to action; organisational leadership; and exemplary papers describing professional leadership. The authors query why the leadership literature is sparse and inexplicit and respond by using the theme of ‘dual citizenship’ to explore the issue from a psychoanalytic and organisational perspective. The psychoanalytic perspective explores tensions and barriers that may be profession-specific in relation to leadership. The organisational perspective explores the wider literature on leadership, starting with the concept of ‘wicked problems and clumsy solutions’. The authors introduce and describe a ‘leadership stance’ that is compatible with psychoanalytic practice in context. This requires opening up leadership activity to the same scrutiny and reflective practice as clinical work, which provides ways of containing organisational and career anxieties and perplexing clinical problems. This paper is a call to action in regard to integrating leadership into the training and the profession.

Response to the Paper by Michael Garcia (2023) ‘The Psychoanalytic Frame and the Consent Situation: The Child Patient's Position in the Publication Dilemma’

Gillian Sloan Donachy

Gillian Sloan Donachy

NHS Greater Glasgow & Clyde
gmsloan@yahoo.com

Gillian Sloan Donachy  

These few words are a brief response to Garcia's paper, published in the August edition of the Journal (Garcia, 2023). It follows on from the online symposium on ethical publishing that took place in March 2022, and the papers that followed in the December 2022 edition of the Journal, opening up a discussion around how we share the development of clinical practice, technique, and understanding through writing up cases, or aspects of cases, in a safe and ethical manner.

I have been reflecting on this subject for the last two or three months, vacillating between enthusiasm for moving the debate forward or giving up altogether and walking away from it. The former carries energy and enthusiasm at the prospect of engaging with colleagues and peers in a creative way, in order to come up with solutions to the very real problems attached to seeking consent for publication, while the latter reflects the depth and breadth of thinking required to properly engage with this complex issue, the time and energy needed to do it justice, and, not least, the potential for anxiety raised by the different views expressed on the subject. It is clear that there is no easy solution to the problem of obtaining fully informed and freely given consent, including sharing of a draft prior to publication being agreed.

Garcia is clear in his view that the ‘consent situation’ is not possible without disrupting or harming the psychoanalytic frame, including the transference relationship. I agree that, at certain points of a psychoanalytic intervention, asking for consent could be disruptive and even harmful, thus the need to think carefully about this. However, I suggest that it is possible for the psychoanalytic frame to remain valued and protected in a situation where consent to publish is being discussed. This may be a point of contention. We could imagine a dividing line with, on one side, those who regard asking for consent to publish as harmful and, on the other side, those who see a collaboration with patients on writing up aspects of their work as another opportunity for growth and development. I wonder whether it is possible to continue thinking creatively and collaboratively about how we can work together with our patients to produce an account of the therapeutic process, without disrupting or damaging the work. The Intergenerational Transmission of Military Trauma and Winnicott’s Principle of Being: Confusion in the Sense of Aliveness and Deadness

Yaakov Roitman PHD

Yaakov Roitman

Naomi Shemer, 27, Mazkeret Batya, Israel
roitmany@gmail.com
http://orcid.org/0000-0002-7012-2287

Yaakov Roitman   Clinical psychologist and supervisor working in private practice in Mazkeret Batya, Israel. His areas of interest include Bion, Winnicott, childhood trauma, autistic spectrum disorders, combatant trauma and childhood psychosis.
PTSD, combatant trauma; intergenerational transmission, Winnicott, sense of being

This work elucidates the unconscious destruction of a sense of being as a result of an obliteration (in the first generation due to direct exposure to military trauma) and rejection (in the second generation due to this trauma being intergenerationally transmitted) of the internal connection with the female element - as conceptualised by Winnicott in his book, ‘Playing and Reality’. The rejection of this aspect of the psyche, which is responsible for the experience of aliveness and being, causes the subject significant confusion in the sense of aliveness and deadness. The result is that survivors of both generations become threatened by a sense of aliveness and being - by life itself. Everything that causes a sense of richness, fullness, intensity, a feeling of vitality and existence, is perceived to be a threat, resulting in an unconscious need to reject such states. These dynamics are explored in the case of an adolescent boy who was experiencing anxiety about becoming a paedophile. His fear, as signified by the image of a paedophile, rather than being a response to the difficulties of his developing sexuality, could be understood as connected to his father’s dissociated war trauma (the fear that he might have killed children), and also to a dissociative imperative to obliterate psychic affiliation with a quiet state of being.

Tim Smith

Tim Smith

UK
timsmithchildpsychotherapy@protonmail.com
http://orcid.org/0000-0002-4882-6923

Tim Smith   A full member of the Association of Child Psychotherapists who trained at the Tavistock Centre when it was affiliated with the University of East London. He works in the NHS and in private practice.
Ending, post-analytic phase, personal training analysis, professional survival, psychoanalytic autoethnography

In this paper, the author further explores and theorises themes from a recent autoethnographical essay ‘Dangerous journey: memories of containment in Cuba’ in which he detailed the immediate demanding period that followed the end of his own analysis – an event which occurred some time after the completion of his formal training. To study this very particular time-period in professional life, he draws on literature on endings in child psychotherapy and the progression of personal training analyses in the psychoanalytic professions, while also referencing discussions held with a range of child psychotherapy colleagues. The reader of this paper is invited to enquire why there are no child psychotherapy publications and a near-void in wider psychoanalytic publications on this important caesura, coupled with a lack of descriptions of the challenges of working in current NHS systems. The author also draws on his experiences to provide a brief, general commentary on such challenges. He hopes that the paper may encourage further writing in the profession on the place of personal analyses within (and often for a time after) the training – especially the possible meanings when ending them – and more broadly of their enduring place in the lives of child psychotherapists post-terminus.

The editorial for the last issue was written by Journal editor Maria Papadima, in which she announced that she is moving on after eight years of tireless service. Elizabeth Edginton

Elizabeth Edginton

3 Worcester Street, Oxford OX1 2BX, UK
eedginton@hotmail.com

Elizabeth Edginton   Qualified as a child and adolescent psychotherapist at the Birmingham Trust for Psychoanalytic Psychotherapy (BTPP) in 2010. She was research lead at the Northern School of Child and Adolescent Psychotherapy from 2011 to 2016 where she was the chief investigator leading the TIGA-CUB feasibility RCT, funded by the National Institute of Health Research (NIHR Research for Patient Benefit Programme PB-PG-0614-34002). Since 2010, she has also worked in Sure Start, CAMHS, and at the Anna Freud Centre and the University of Warwick, and she currently works at the Counselling Service of the University of Oxford and in private practice.
Child and adolescent, research, psychoanalytic psychotherapy, randomised controlled trial (RCT), TIGA-CUB

Using the country house poetry of the English Civil War as a metaphor, this article traces some of the key debates in child and adolescent psychoanalytic psychotherapy (CAPPT) research over the last 25 years. It identifies three main trends: initial confidence that child and adolescent psychoanalytic psychotherapists (CAPPTs) could apply their existing theoretical methods to empirical research; recognition of the need to use qualitative methodology and to engage with quantitative approaches; and a period of retrenchment, with particular questioning of the use of randomised controlled trial (RCT) methodology. The article also reports the results of a service evaluation undertaken subsequent to the feasibility Trial on Inter-Generational Attachment and Children Undergoing Behaviour problems (TIGA-CUB) to determine whether to proceed to a large-scale, definitive trial, and the inclusion of TIGA-CUB in an on-going, innovative research project on RCT methodology. The article concludes that, if CAPPTs want RCT methodology more appropriate to their ways of working, the profession and the Association of Child Psychotherapists (ACP) will need to develop a more pro-research environment, as well as career pathways which combine clinical work and publicly funded research.

Saul Hillman   Senior research fellow at the Anna Freud Centre and an honorary lecturer at University College London. He teaches and supervises across several different postgraduate programmes through both institutions. Within his research role, he has primarily managed and worked on studies around attachment and mentalization. Much of his work has been in the field of children who were either looked-after or adopted. His research interests are attachment, mentalization, measure development, looked-after children, adoption and trauma.
Parental representations of the child, high-risk parents, MBT intervention, children under 5s, qualitative single case study

This paper explores the parental representations of the child, through the case study of one participant in a mentalization-based intervention for parents of young children aged one – two years old, involved with the child welfare system as a result of their child's maltreatment. A single mother's representations of the child are analysed during the programme, through a qualitative lens. Narrative Processes Coding System (NPCS) and Thematic Analysis (TA) are used in combination, to elicit the mother's representations by identifying language modes and themes from her narratives about both her own and other children. The maternal representations of the child appeared to be less negative as the programme reached its end. The mother's reflexive language grew significantly in the middle phase of the programme and regressed during the last phase. However, the combined use of NPCS and TA showed an overall richer and less negative portrayal of the child during the ending phase. These findings suggest that during the course of the programme, the mother's journey through her representations of the child, was characterised by progressions and regressions. There was also an emotional richness in the last phase of the programme that indicates the mother's engagement in the group and her overall positive journey towards the development and the strengthening of a less negative representation of the child. Despite its limitations, this study hopes to provide insights for clinicians establishing and promoting interventions that aim to empower parents to clearly see their children.

This paper explores the challenge of establishing a meaningful connection between a neurotypical therapist and a neurodiverse patient who inhabit different Umwelts, that is, perceptual worlds.1 It discusses how addressing anxiety is crucial in preventing communication difficulties from escalating for individuals with autism who may have heightened stress due to an overgrown amygdala. The paper emphasises the importance of responding to individual differences in sensory and perceptual experiences to promote effective communication and positive outcomes in therapy.

Her research interests include psychoanalysis and education, trauma, and parent–child separation.
Peer groups, psychoanalytic groups, teachers’ groups, early education, reflective account, work discussion groups

In the field of education, work discussion groups focus on teachers’ emotional experience with their students and offer a safe environment in which professionals can freely interact and explore the dynamics and relationships in their workplace. A psychoanalytic therapist usually leads them. They are considered particularly important for preschool education, as young children provoke intense emotional reactions in adults. Although the effectiveness of work discussion groups in preschools has been positively evaluated, their application is considered financially unaffordable. This paper presents the function of a work discussion peer group in preschool education, that is with a preschool teacher as facilitator. To do so, the facilitator's point of view is presented in this paper in the form of a reflective account. A group consisting of six kindergarten teachers was formed. It met for seven sessions. After each group meeting, the facilitator kept a reflective diary. The topics of the meetings included the facilitator's struggle to be seen as a peer, the group dynamics, the development of the group and the importance of supervision, which are all discussed.

Hannah Barnes’ troubling book on the collapse of the Tavistock's Gender Service is both a fascinating and painful read. It tells the story of the events that unfolded as the Gender Identity Development Service (GIDS) evolved from a largely therapeutic service providing mostly talking therapies for young people struggling with their gender identity, to one in which medical interventions, specifically puberty blockers, appeared to become the treatment of choice after only a few assessment sessions. Hannah Barnes, a BBC Newsnight journalist by profession, has written a book that takes a deep dive into the cultural issues, both within the Tavistock and Portman Trust and GIDS itself, as well as in wider society, that drove this change and the impact that it had.

In writing this review, I am aware of the risk of stepping into a deeply polarised debate, steeped in ideological belief that does not lend itself to nuanced dialogue. This is in part because it feels impossible to separate a review of the book from that of the story it tells, and I am likely to be seen to be taking a stance one way or the other, whether or not I believe I am. In this debate, those giving a view tend to be experienced as either for or against, trans-allies or trans-phobic, and this does not easily enable a thoughtful, curious dialogue.

The book is divided into chapters that outline chronologically, and in great detail, the course of events that took place between the early 2000s and 2022, interspersed with personal stories of young people who had themselves been patients at GIDS, some of whose experiences had been nothing but positive and others who had much more complicated outcomes. These stories, while in some ways anecdotal as they represent a tiny fraction of the young people seen in the service, bring to life the issues and complexities at the heart of the controversy surrounding GIDS: how can anyone know whether the gender dysphoria experienced by a child reflects their true identity or is a fluid, changing exploration of their gender and, perhaps, sexuality, in the way that so many things are fluid in childhood and adolescence? And if this cannot be known for certain, is it ethical to offer medical interventions that may have life changing side-effects to children whose bodies are still developing?

Michael Rustin  

Forgiving is both a deeply normal human activity, and yet one which may take place only rarely and with considerable difficulty. This valuable and interesting collection of essays sets out to explore the meaning of forgiveness as a state of mind and as an act. As a concept it 168 has not been widely discussed in the psychoanalytic culture, compared for example with envy, jealousy or resentment, and it is not easy to locate its place in its main theoretical lexicon. This is a partial absence, which the authors of this book have set out to address.

The normality and necessity of forgiveness in human lives are described early in the book by Hiroshi Amino, in his observations on the experiences of infancy. The experiences of frustration and anger are unavoidable, indeed ever-present, in infant life, as the satisfactions of mother's attention, and of the breast, are from time to time denied, and the infant feels persecuted and attacked as this happens. Mother and others who care for an infant will from time to time feel rejected or hated in turn. But mothers and babies are both frequently and easily forgiven when good feelings are restored, and it is only when a relationship is going badly that a parent finds it difficult to forgive their infant for its periods of anger or rejection, or an infant loses trust in the goodness of its parent. It is important to bear this everyday good human experience in mind when considering how difficult it can be in many other circumstances for imputed injuries to be forgiven.

This book does not set out a unified theoretical argument, proceeding to illustrate its applications to experience through deduced instances. Instead, its authors each examine the phenomenon of forgiveness, and the dispositions to exact revenge or grievance, which are its antithesis, in their own ways, with contexts of application related to their own interests and fields of expertise. Karl Figlio makes the fullest reference to previous psychoanalytic writing, and there are interesting theoretical explorations in several chapters, including those by Aleksandra Novakovic and John Steiner. One can say that what emerges is a presentation of Wittgensteinian ‘family resemblances’, describing related experiences of injury, grievance, and forgiveness, and theoretical accounts of these. These provide many ideas and instances to reflect on. In this way, the collection may be seen as a work in progress towards a definitive psychoanalytic understanding of the place of forgiveness among human dispositions of mind, both conscious and unconscious.

The author presents the issue of the development of internal space, as a function of the relationship of intimacy and synchrony with the caregiver, with the purpose of rendering more tolerable the experience of space outside the body. This paper argues that if this relationship does not stabilise by the end of the first year of life, an absence of representation of an internal space in the unidimensional realm might ensue. The psychoanalytic treatment of autistic children offers windows to certain developmental challenges associated with the representation of both internal and external spaces, the consequent development of dimensionality and its deviations. The case of a young autistic child in the first year of her four-session-a-week analysis is described as an illustration of the child’s struggle to overcome precipitation anxiety around the experience of falling by using her movements in the external space. The child’s autistic defences and deficits at first functioned to keep her in a liquid state, and later denied gravity by means of repetitive movements of her body while exploring the space of the analyst’s room. Her mouth was experienced as a hole to be completely blocked with either food or a pacifier, preventing exchanges with the analyst. Her subsequent compulsive use of strings in activities revealed at the same time the search for links, and her difficulty connecting and establishing communication. At the end, the analyst realised an archaic equivalence between their room and body, as a ‘concrete transference’, revealing the child’s attachment and motivation to explore it, which could be interpreted as an affective link between the analyst and patient.

The front cover of this new edition of Graham Music’s excellent and inspiring ‘Nurturing natures’ has a ‘puff’ from Jeremy Holmes saying: ‘Music is the David Attenborough of child development research’. At first glance, I was rather startled by that but having read the book I can see just what Professor Holmes had in mind. Something that most of us had only a faint awareness of - the depths and breadth of research into many aspects of child development - is shown to us by Music in a way that enables us to see and wonder, making the complicated child development research it describes lively and accessible. Music can be our trusted guide because although he is writing about research gathered from so many unfamiliar areas of study, the whole book is suffused by the way he thinks as a clinician, and his concern to introduce thinking, which therapists and other practitioners might find helpful in their work.

I wrote a review of the first edition of this book and at the time, when research in all its forms was much less embedded into the child psychotherapist’s way of thinking, I thought that the book was rather helpful, suggesting that I didn’t have to read ‘all that stuff’ because Graham Music had read it for me and given me an overview. Perhaps, because over the years our profession has developed a more embracing attitude to research - both our own and that of allied disciplines - I now find myself more interested in following up on various studies that he cites.

This book uses much of what was in earlier editions but has been massively updated, both in terms of the studies cited, and with some chapters, such as those on gender, race and culture, attachment and adolescence, more substantially re-written. Music acknowledges, for example, the cultural bias of previous research on attachment, commenting on ‘how transient and fleeting scientific and moral certainties can be,’ (p. 11).

The information is also presented in a more visually engaging way: there are numerous pictures and diagrams - while I found most of the pictures pleasing, and occasionally moving, I was less impressed by the diagrams. Some of them seemed rather simplistic which, together with the questions for discussion at the end of each chapter, made me wonder who the reader that Music was aiming for was. How do Adolescents End Open-Ended Psychoanalytic Psychotherapy? Exploring Dropout in a Community-Based Clinic

Greta Steponaityte and Sally O’Keeffe

Sally O’Keeffe

London, UK
greta.steponaityte@brentcentre.org.uk

Newcastle-Upon-Tyne, UK

Sally O’Keeffe   Mental health research fellow in the NIHR Applied Research Collaboration North East and North Cumbria, based at Newcastle University. Her research focuses on mental health support for children and families, and she has a particular interest in interventions for youth depression and self-harm.
Adolescent, dropout, psychoanalytic psychotherapy, therapy, young people

Dropout from psychotherapy among adolescents is a common occurrence. Adolescents’ need for independence can be in direct conflict with therapeutic relationships, particularly in open-ended psychotherapy where endings need to be negotiated. The present study was a service evaluation, which aimed to identify how open-ended once-weekly psychoanalytic psychotherapy ends with adolescents, and whether dropout could be predicted from a range of adolescent and treatment factors. The sample comprised 443 adolescents, aged 14-24, who had received psychoanalytic psychotherapy in a community-based clinic. Logistic regression was used to estimate the effects of predictors on the odds of dropout. Adolescents were categorised based on how treatment ended: adolescents’ unilateral decision (43%), mutually agreed between adolescent and therapist (27%), initiated by changed external circumstances such as relocation (23%) or a referral to another service (6%). Younger adolescents and those from more disadvantaged backgrounds were most at risk of dropout. Missed sessions early in treatment were also predictive of dropout. Neither therapist change nor the number of services was significantly associated with dropout. This study shows that dropout is a frequent occurrence in open-ended psychoanalytic psychotherapy. Further research is needed to explore how young people at risk of dropout can be better supported to attend treatment to ensure they receive the maximum benefits. Moreover, research is required to identify how therapists can optimally respond to missed sessions, to avoid subsequent dropout and to facilitate positive and appropriate treatment endings.

Natasha Stubbs  

Having no prior knowledge of Juliet Mitchell’s pioneering work on psychoanalysis and feminism, I set out to review her latest book, ‘Fratriarchy: the sibling trauma and the law of the mother’, with little more than a curiosity about the title. Just a few pages in, I became somewhat daunted by the task ahead of me. Even though there were times whilst reading this book that I felt that I was wading through theory thicker than treacle, I can promise that both the journey and destination offer many rewards. What emerges in Mitchell’s volume is a fascinating exploration of how the toddler’s experience of being usurped by the new baby (in reality or phantasy) is a rite of passage in early childhood that provides the structural foundation of lateral relationships within society.

Central to Mitchell’s theory is the concept of the ubiquitous foundational trauma, the ‘Law of the Mother’ (as opposed to the developmentally later Oedipal ‘Law of the Father’). The toddler is overwhelmed by the urge both to love the new baby sibling to the point of assimilation (incest) and to exterminate it (murder). Under this Law, the mother prohibits the toddler against murder and incest with a new sibling through threats of abandonment if her Law is not adhered to. The ‘Law of the Father’ lies on the vertical axis between generations, whereas in the ‘Law of the Mother’:

‘do not bite the breast’ - moves to the horizontal family where a new requirement - ‘do not bite your sister or brother who is my new baby’ morphs into what will become a dramatic prohibition. The mother’s vertical family authority, her rules and regulations and her lateral social prohibitions are all enjoyed under her all-prevalent task of introducing reality. In psychoanalytic thinking, because inducing reality is the providence of the mother, the importance of reality was, for a long time, missed … the mother’s crucial role … was, and is, omitted. (p. 43)

Editorial

Rachel Acheson

Rachel Acheson

rachel.acheson@childpsychotherapy.org.uk

Rachel Acheson  

This issue marks the final instalment of the Journal's 50th volume. First appearing in 1963, 14 years after the founding of the ACP, it began as a ‘“local”, in house affair’ (Barrows, 2004, p. xii), developing into a leading Taylor & Francis publication, with international readers and contributors. There is no doubt that for ACP child psychotherapists the Journal holds an important position, historically and currently. As Editor, I am often struck by the strong feelings it evokes in fellow ACP members – whether of affection, guilt, or admiration! Despite early issues being at times hard to come by, we are fortunate that the back catalogue is now only a click away, as from 2007 all previous issues were made available online. I have no doubt that we have a previous Journal Editor to thank for this, along with many other aspects of how the Journal runs today.

In the foreword to ‘Key papers from the Journal of Child Psychotherapy’ (Barrows, 2004), Maria Rhode writes about ‘the excitement with which my fellow trainees and I in the late 1960s and early 1970s opened each issue’ and how the papers within the pages ‘conveyed the sense that fundamental issues related to the practice of child psychotherapy were being thought through for the first time’ (p. vii). I recognise the feeling Rhode describes, and also the style she attributes to early JCP papers. In a recent conversation with Miranda Passey, a member of the Journal Group, she described the papers as sometimes ‘being written with quite a degree of certainty, like brave little boats being sent out to sea’ (personal communication). This may be characteristic of a fledgling discipline, and though I imagine there are ideas and attitudes shared in early volumes of the Journal that we would not stand by today (see Eriksen's review paper within this issue for some interesting examples), they no doubt reflect the development of our profession and our changing society.

Although a lot of time and effort goes into producing the Journal in 2024, it has been interesting to hear from past Journal editors how technological advances have eased the load – sometimes quite literally. Teresa Bailey (personal communication) recalled how, during her 16 years on the board, the Journal underwent the transition from analogue to digital. As a so-called ‘digital native’ it is hard to imagine running the Journal without the use of computers and email, and her descriptions of sending papers back and forth by post, carrying heavy bags of papers to Journal Group meetings, and getting submissions on incompatible floppy discs, felt both quaint and hugely admirable. One of the valuable aspects of the Journal for me is the sense of connection it fosters between those who engage with it, but I imagine this felt all the stronger when the effort to do so was greater. Barrows (2004) writes that ‘Child psychotherapy – quite rightly – “stands on the shoulders of giants” in the sense that it builds on the creative work of its founders’. I hope the Journal continues to advance in this way, both through the publications of our authors, and the development of the Journal as a whole.

Infantile Perspectives on the Replacement Child

Mary Short

Mary Short

Saintfield Road, Belfast BT8 8BH, UK
Mary.short@belfasttrust.hscni.net

Mary Short   Consultant child and adolescent psychiatrist in child and adolescent mental health services (CAMHS), and as a parent-infant psychotherapist in a perinatal service, both within the Belfast Trust in Northern Ireland. She also works with children, adolescents and adults in private practice. She qualified as a child psychotherapist at the Tavistock Clinic in 2012 and as a parent-infant psychoanalytic psychotherapist at the Anna Freud Centre in 2020. She is an adult and child analyst and a member of the Northern Ireland and the British Psychoanalytic Societies.
Parent-infant psychoanalytic psychotherapy, early intervention, replacement child, play, mourning, metaphoric function

This paper tells the story of the work of a parent-infant psychoanalytic psychotherapist with an infant girl and her mother, from the age of four to 19 months old. It became clear, very quickly, that she was a replacement child. She was born four years after the death of her profoundly disabled brother and before her mother had begun the process of mourning her dead son. The mother was struggling to see the infant as a person in her own right and felt that she wanted her daughter to be a reincarnation of her dead brother. Although the infant was always dressed as a girl, there was also something boyish about her presentation. The work centred around us playing together and helping her mother to see her as a person in her own right, as well as observing and trying to make sense of the infant's play. The therapist used her metaphoric function to hypothesise what the infant might be trying to understand in her play, especially with two identical plastic oranges that were the same and yet different. What emerged was that the mother was herself an identical twin, who never felt fully separated from her twin sister, and always felt that she was two people. An interpretation to the infant that perhaps she also thought that she needed to be two people, herself but also her dead brother, was met with a confirmatory response from the infant; it felt pivotal in elucidating for both mother and infant their respective challenges in the wake of the death of their son/sibling. The paper illustrates the importance of early intervention, of both observing and playing with infants and young children; and the importance of the therapist's use of metaphor, which could be viewed as an inductive statement, summarising a guess about inner reality expressed in a skewed or displaced way.

Rachel Acheson

Rachel Acheson

rachel.acheson@childpsychotherapy.org.uk

Rachel Acheson  

I begin my first editorial as Editor-in-Chief by extending my thanks to Alexandra de Rementeria who I succeed in this role. Alex rather bravely took on the job in 2020 during the coronavirus pandemic when many people were feeling saturated with their responsibilities at work and at home. The Journal had been understaffed for some time and as a result it was behind schedule and morale was low. Alex worked hard with Maria Papadima (then Journal Editor) to ‘steady the ship’, and later went on to make significant contributions in developing thinking and debate within our pages on ethical publishing and equality, diversity and inclusion. Alex is a great champion of others, and I feel lucky to have been on the receiving end of this. I have learnt a lot from the sincerity of her depth of thinking, her capacity for gratitude, and her bravery. I wish her all the best as she takes on her new role as principal child and adolescent psychotherapist at Lambeth CAMHS.

This is a ‘general’ issue, meaning the papers have not been collected or organised around a particular theme, and are being published together simply because they are ‘ready’. It happens that this issue is noteworthy both in that it tackles issues that are challenging, such as gender dysphoria, and also in that we have contributions from authors who live in parts of the world currently at war. As a Journal we take no political position but do wish to support all therapists who continue to try and think about the minds and experience of others, especially children, young people and their families, while forces around them seek to obliterate such thinking.

The first paper in this issue is by Vera Fonseca, who writes from Brazil. She builds on the work of Klein and Meltzer in thinking about the development of our sense of space, both internally and externally, and how this has been compromised in children who go on to be diagnosed as autistic. This, she hypothesises, is due in part to their failure to introject the containing functions of their caregivers. While I found this paper theoretically challenging, the thinking was brought to light by the clinical material, through which Fonseca attempts to understand the play of a young autistic girl who displays a high degree of bodily omnipotence. This paper was originally submitted without the required informed consent for its publication, but the author subsequently sought this, and details the process in a footnote to the paper. I commend them for being brave enough to take this step, which has allowed us as readers to benefit more fully from their thinking.

When Autism and Adolescence Meet: A Combined Psychoanalytic and Developmental Perspective on Some Clinical Work with Autistic Adolescents

Dahlia W. Levy PHD

Dahlia W. Levy

Israel
dwlevy99@gmail.com

Dahlia W. Levy   PhD from the City University of New York and works as a clinical psychologist in Israel in private practice and recently in the Resilience Centre in the south of Israel. Over the past 18 years, she has worked for OTI, the Israeli Autism Association, first in the special kindergartens and as team lead and supervisor for one of the in-school treatment programmes and more recently as a teacher and as a member of a task force on suicide assessment, prevention and intervention in the autistic population.
Autism, adolescence, psychoanalytic focus, social struggles, emotional regulation, parents

This paper explores the meeting of autism and adolescent developmental processes from a combined psychoanalytic and developmental perspective. Meltzer's four states of minds or ‘communities’, and the back and forth movements between them during the adolescent period, are described and serve as the theoretical underpinnings for the exploration of adolescent processes in the autistic individual. Motivation, or the desire and emotional capacity to encounter novelty and change, as the engine for movement between the four different states of mind, is also explored. An emphasis is placed on two key characteristics of the autistic experience – sensory/emotional overload and social struggle – and the impact and implications these have on the emotional capacity to cope with the many changes that characterise this transitional period. Clinical examples are used to illustrate the young person's neurodivergent experience and to encourage clinical techniques that are better adapted to this experience and that hopefully ease the burden placed on these young people to meet neurotypical expectations. The concluding section of this paper will offer some thoughts on the experiences of the parents of autistic adolescents.

I suspect that the first (2008) and second (2011) editions of this book by the psychologist and Tavistock trained child and adolescent psychotherapist were very different. In the introduction and conclusion to the third edition, Blake, who is based in Australia, details how he has changed his clinical thinking and practice over the decades since he first trained. At times reading this book, I felt as if I was closely following the evolution of a senior therapist wanting to properly learn from clinical experience. Broadly, Blake addresses three aspects of child and adolescent psychoanalytic psychotherapy. Namely, the place of interpretation, the centrality of play and the use of transference/countertransference. He uses recent developments in psychoanalysis and contiguous fields to argue clearly for a more relational approach to clinical work with children and adolescents.

This book is being used in training the next generation of child psychotherapists in Australia and one can see why. It has crystal clear descriptions of complex psychoanalytic thinking, key summary points and suggested further reading at the end of each of the chapters. It would be wrong, however, to consider it a simple book or a primer. Blake distils the research and clinical thinking of many eminent writers in order to challenge the status quo. For example, the title borrows Ogden's quote about operating not at the epistemological but the ontological level: ‘making the conscious unconscious’.

Antonio Santamaría (1930–2013) was a pioneer and leading voice of psychoanalysis in Latin America. The A-Santamaría Association was set up in his honour by his daughter Jani 543 Santamaría Linares to continue her father's love of psychoanalytic learning which, from my very positive experience of her, she also inherited in droves.

This is a highly stimulating collection of papers that grapple in a refreshing, sometimes novel way, with Bion's original texts, some 40 years after his death. In her editor's ‘Introduction’ Santamaría Linares describes the book's context: how in 1997, Bion's first daughter Parthenope – a talented analyst in her own right – organised the inaugural International Bion Conference in Italy to mark the centennial of her father's birth. In the spirit of this tradition, the A-Santamaría Association was organising the first Mexican International Bion Conference, due to be held in 2022, when preparations were interrupted, as with all human activity on the planet, by COVID-19. However, within this dark and unusual circumstance, a series of creative online seminars were conceived, bringing together Bion scholars and an audience of interested analysts and psychotherapists from around the world to present and debate their readings and contemporary applications of Bion's work.

Attending myself, I was invited to deliver a seminar of my own, focused on my research on Bion's first autobiography The Long Weekend (1982/2014). Curiously, I noticed I developed a sore throat and felt strangely tired shortly before speaking; though with a glass of water at my side, my presentation went well. Ironically, I received my first positive lateral flow test the following day, almost two years into the pandemic (this despite having worked face-to-face, with the required PPE, in child mental health clinics in London since the outset)! Well, I was lucky enough to suffer only briefly with what were very mild symptoms. It is the papers from this fascinating set of seminars that are published in this volume.

A brief discussion with a colleague, several months ago, set me on a road of discovery, one which has proven to be complex in terms of the multitude of information and research being reported and presented within the field of epigenetics in relation to the transmission of intergenerational trauma. The discussion in question had centred around a report, within mainstream media, of research into the transmission of intergenerational trauma in mice, conducted by Otaru et al. (2024, included in the abstracts below). The research findings had shown biological evidence of stress in early life affecting subsequent offspring and increasing the offspring's risk of developing psychiatric and cardiometabolic diseases across generations. Having been aware of the research by Painter et al. Intergenerational trauma (where trauma is an event in the subject's life defined by: its intensity, the subject's incapacity to respond adequately to it, and the upheaval and long-lasting effects that it brings about in the psychical organisation (Laplanche & Pontalis, 1988)) acknowledges that the exposure to extremely adverse events can impact individuals to such a great extent that the post traumatic symptomatology is experienced by subsequent generations. Intergenerational trauma (also referred to as historical trauma, multigenerational trauma, secondary traumatisation and transgenerational trauma) is a term that is widely accepted within clinical practice. It is also a term that appears to be accepted within the general population, thus taking it beyond the boundaries of clinical and research practice. The Experience of Puberty1

Shirley Hoxter

Shirley Hoxter

Shirley Hoxter  

Introduction

The specific feature which differentiates the adolescent from people of other ages is the experience of puberty, and much of the adolescent's behaviour in the community may be seen as an external expression of the unconscious anxieties and conflicts aroused by pubertal sexual development. It also appears that some of the community's reactions to adolescents express the anxiety of the adult when faced with the fact that a new generation is attaining sexual maturity. An adolescent girl reflected a widespread attitude when saying ‘I know what juvenile delinquency means, but I am not sure which word means “young person” and which word means “criminal”’. The constant stories of teenage violence and teenage sexuality and the reactions of outraged protest, force upon one the realisation that prominent sections of the adolescent population and of the adult population alike are engaged in the warlike activity of acting out their oedipal rivalry. This is often conducted in conformity to stereotyped patterns of conflict which enable both parties to avoid experiencing guilt and personal responsibility for the intense feelings of hostility and envy arising from their mutual sexual rivalry. Sometimes the conflict occurs on a vast scale and most of the population is drawn into participating in the melodrama at least vicariously. Or it may initially be conducted as a one-man war. A boy telephoned me late one night saying ‘I have urgent news to tell you. I am at war with she L.C.C.’ This was followed by tenacious and partially successful efforts to get myself and other members of the Clinic staff to act in conjunction with him and to become involved in conflict with many County Council officials. It was only just possible to prevent him from extending his war to the police and to Interpol.

The physical maturation of the adolescent, with its greatly increased sexual drives, is simultaneously accompanied by a resurgence of the imperious feelings and phantasies which previously characterised the object relations of early childhood. The adolescent is faced with the task of relinquishing his parents as his original sexual objects and turning to others outside the family. This leads to further difficulties when impulses stemming from the infantile aspects of his sexuality continue to dominate his behaviour, both with his peers and with adults. The adolescent has the physical capacity to put into action much which would appear mainly as phantasy in the young child. He can really attack, destroy, rob, murder or commit suicide and he can really have sexual experiences of a heterosexual, homosexual or perverse nature. The young child can be protected and controlled by his parents, but the parents of the adolescent are powerless to do either if he opposes them with full force. Emily Morgan   A Child and Adolescent Psychoanalytic Psychotherapist in Wakefield CAMHS. She is a tutor on the Clinical Training and the Psychoanalytic Observational Studies course at the Northern School of Child and Adolescent Psychotherapy (NSCAP).

In writing this commentary on a lesser known, yet classic Hoxter paper, I found myself wondering about the origins of its title, ‘The experience of puberty’ and feeling how little these few words convey the clinical insight and riches within. ‘The experience of’ in the title, to my mind, gives an impression of a more static concept of adolescence with ‘puberty’ at the centre. The tumultuous transition and state of flux that is the adolescent period is anything but generic and fixed. Adolescence starts, in many ways, with the physical maturation and psychosexual advent of puberty, and yet once physical puberty is ‘over’, adolescent states of mind remain with us long after the chronological teenage years have passed.

The understanding that during puberty the rate and speed of physiological, neurological and physical changes are so rapid that they are only comparable to those that occur in the womb, is not new. These physical, hormonal and neurological changes carry with them psychological states, which demand expression through a maturing sexual body. The development of the sexual body, which for some can feel imposed, ushers in the resurgence of infantile anxieties and phantasies. When working with early adolescents in the consulting room as child and adolescent psychotherapists (CAPTs) we acutely see, and feel, the connections between the infantile drives and impulses, now needing to be newly negotiated and modified. In this paper, Hoxter seems to have found a way to convey, with sharp alertness, how the resurgence of the infantile feelings of her patients within a newly developing sexual body may be thought about and additionally addresses aspects of technique in the work.

In an informative and contemporary commentary on Hoxter's paper given by Bradley (2017) in this Journal, a brief account of the historical and cultural framework to the idea of puberty in Britian in the 1960s sets the scene for Hoxter's writing. Not only is Bradley's paper helpful in placing Hoxter's writing in context, that being a time of social and political renewal post-war, but in bringing our attention to what an extraordinary period of generative thinking this was for the child and adolescent psychotherapy profession. As I re-read this rich and cogently argued paper, memories of my contact with Shirley Hoxter in the early 1980s surfaced – her strong presence, along with her depth and clarity of thought. Nataliya Zueva presents us with a very interesting addition to our journal. Not only is an article on the role of the father of interest, not least for its rarity, she takes a very particular view of fathers as part of parental couples. Aware that the role has a diverse potential occupancy in modern Western societies, brought by what she terms the ‘decline of the traditional family structure’, her focus is on ‘heteronormative families’ (2024, p. 213). Thus, her discussion is of male role holders. However, before beginning her discussion she acknowledges that sometimes his participation may be limited to a part in the act of conception (coitus or assisted pregnancy through sperm donation). With his absence in, for example, parenting by single mothers, or same-sex female parental couples, the paternal function ‘might then be provided by a good enough “other”, an alternative parental figure.’ (2024, p. 213). All this is straightforward enough until one seeks conceptual help in order to understand how this role is experienced by families across this diverse spectrum. It is then that one remembers that, regardless of this diversity, even the traditional role of the father is not so easily defined within the contemporary object-relations literature. Arguably, and indeed paradoxically, its lack of definition hinges upon the very term Zueva uses to describe her families – heteronormative.

I am not clear what Zueva means by saying her paper ‘is based on a heteronormative position, even though we are all witnessing that a significant shift has taken place in stereotypical gender-role thinking’ (2024, p. 213). For me, this read as her stubbornly seeing heteronormativity, despite her acknowledgement of a decline in traditional family structure, which also includes the effect of the role being potentially occupied by female parents. But throughout her discussions, she does not otherwise suggest hetero is normative. Far from it, and so it might be safer to suggest that she is thinking not so much about heteronormativity as she is about the heterosexual parental couple, of which the father who remains after conception is a heterosexual male. In other words, whilst I am not sure what she means by heteronormative, her lack of clarity leaves me uncertain; poised between wondering whether she is using the term as descriptive or prescriptive. If this is her ambiguity it adds to the richness of her paper, because it opens up a debate about her meaning, which has a parallel experience when one attempts to find the father within the contemporary object-relations literature.

Clara Louis  

Hoxter's paper, titled ‘The experience of puberty’ (1964), provides a comprehensive account of the tumultuous transition from childhood to adulthood. The detailed clinical vignettes clearly demonstrate the depth and complexity of each patient's experience of puberty, and their phantasies and feelings towards their developing sexuality. There is an abundance of themes within the paper which could be thought about in greater detail. However, for the purpose of this commentary, I will focus on some of the therapeutic techniques Hoxter utilises within her work with adolescents, with a particular focus on working with the transference. I will also consider how this relates to my experience as a trainee child and adolescent psychotherapist.

Despite working in child and adolescent mental health services (CAMHS) for many years prior to embarking on my psychoanalytic journey, working in the transference has been a new experience. Transference takes place within the emotional relationship between the patient and therapist and is a central concept of psychoanalysis. It is a process of communication whereby the patient's psychic world is re-experienced and relived in the present (Klein, 1952; Spillius, 1988). Working in the transference enables the therapist to respond to and interpret the emotional immediacy of the patient, and to make containing interpretations within the therapeutic relationship. Through clinical work within my role as a trainee child psychotherapist and through working with my analyst, I have experienced first-hand the profoundness of interpretations made in the transference. From these experiences, I have developed a deep appreciation of how fundamental working in the transference is for the therapeutic relationship, and for the progression of the clinical work.

However, as a trainee, I have found it quite challenging at times to remain working in the transference. Until 2023 he was the Academic Director of the Independent Child Psychotherapy training, a collaboration between IPCAPA, the Anna Freud Centre and UCL. He was a research lead on the IMPACT study and was one of the authors of the treatment guide, Short Term Psychoanalytic Psychotherapy for Adolescents with Depression (Routledge, 2016).
Adolescence, depression, psychoanalytic psychotherapy, process research, short-term psychoanalytic psychotherapy

This paper explores the psychotherapy process in a short-term psychoanalytic treatment (STPP) with a depressed adolescent. The empirical case study draws on both quantitative and qualitative data to examine the development of the psychotherapy process over time. 15 of the 29 audio recorded therapy sessions with a 16-year-old boy were sampled at intervals across the treatment. Session transcripts were coded using the Adolescent Psychotherapy Q-Set (APQ) and data analysed descriptively to compare characteristics of the process across the three treatment phases – beginning, middle, and ending. Descriptive statistics are supported with session extracts. Analysis of the APQ data suggests change in the patient's presentation across the therapy. In the early stages, he appeared withdrawn and made minimal responses to the therapist's attempts to work together; in the middle phase, he became more engaged, more able to talk about feelings, and more active in the sessions; and this was reflected in a less depressed presentation in the final phase. The therapist maintained a consistent therapeutic approach across all phases: supportive, non-judgemental, and working to make sense of the young person's experiences, looking for patterns and inviting curiosity about how things might be understood differently. Despite increased engagement in the therapy, depressive symptoms remained in the clinical range.

Child psychotherapy, racism, Whiteness, early Oedipal struggles, othering

This paper takes as its premise the idea that transferential phenomena emerge out of the endless interactions between the wider social context, including myriad social injustices, and the inter and intra psychic events psychoanalytic therapists are more familiar with thinking about. Freud's was a neuro-psycho-social model of development, with the interrelationship between internal life and social practices carefully mapped in ‘Totem and Taboo’ (1913) and ‘Civilisation and Its Discontents’ (S. Freud, 1930). However, what Freud left undone, and is still only nascent in its development, is the work of mapping how this interaction between internal and external, between psycho and social, manifests in the consulting room. Focusing on race, as one aspect of identity that powerfully impacts transferential phenomena, the paper presents accounts of clinical events, one disguised, one fictionalised, to explore the meaning of the author's own Whiteness in this context. Using a Kleinian and post-Kleinian understanding of very early Oedipal struggles, ‘Whiteness’ is formulated as an anti-developmental merger with the ideal breast.

The paper draws on fictionalised composite case histories to explore themes in psychotherapeutic work with gender questioning and transgender young people. Gender and transgender are examined from psychoanalytic, cultural and philosophical perspectives. It is argued that the meaning of gender and transgender as an identity is rooted in unconscious processes and patterns of relationship. An ethical argument is made for a therapeutic stance, which remains curious about and receptive to complexity in therapeutic work with gender questioning young people and their families. The need for the therapist to be aware of their own blind spots in work with gender questioning young people is discussed.

Child psychotherapy, elopement, hope, autism, Tustin, Alvarez

Our separateness from the other is the ‘basic agony’, the ‘original heartbreak’ of the human condition, according to Frances Tustin’s thinking. The ways we deal with this heartbreak form the foundation through which relationships, self-experience and wellbeing are built and developed. The following paper describes a child’s journey, from omnipotent encapsulation, through the extremes of heartbreak - the child’s, as well as his parents’ and the therapist’s - to liveliness and hope. Tustin teaches us the meaning and experience of encapsulation, the delicate balance between ‘hard’ and ‘soft’ needed in the therapeutic stance, the extremes of despair, hurt, cruelty and heartbreak that are met with along the way, as well as the possibility of hope even in dire situations. Holding on, survival and faith, as well as hope-against-hope, which is the resistance to despair in situations of hopelessness, are needed in order for this broken heart to be somewhat mended and allowed to flourish and to grow.

He served as a consultant psychotherapist and mental health nurse, and held the position of head of the nursing discipline at the Tavistock & Portman NHS Trust from 1998 to 2018. Additionally, he played a pivotal role as one of the founding members of the Fitzjohn’s Service, aimed at treating patients with severe and enduring mental health conditions and/or personality disorders. Throughout his career, Evans has extensively contributed to both writing and teaching. He is the author of three books: ‘Making room for madness in mental health: the psychoanalytic understanding of psychotic communications’, published by Karnac in 2016; ‘Psychoanalytic thinking in mental health settings’, which introduces frontline mental health professionals to psychoanalytic thinking and was published by Routledge in 2020; and his third book, co-written with his wife Susan Evans, titled ‘Gender dysphoria: a therapeutic model for working with children, adolescents, and young adults’, published by Phoenix in 2021.
Gender dysphoria, identity, adolescence, transference

This paper explores clinical work concerning a group of gender-questioning natal males who experienced physical difficulties in childhood. The author argues that these individuals develop a transgender (trans) identity as a defence mechanism against the psychological challenges associated with development, particularly the struggles of forming a distinct mind and identity. Anxieties related to physical health may have contributed to the formation of an anxious attachment to their primary caregiver, perceived as intrusive and demanding. Moreover, these individuals struggle to identify with their fathers, often experiencing them as distant, absent, or unsupportive of their relationship with the mother or other primary caregiver, thereby hindering separation from the primary attachment figure. These early experiences may lead to difficulties in acknowledging and owning their evolving sexuality and aggression, as well as in bearing the necessary guilt associated with separating from the primary caregiver. Consequently, the individual may fantasise about relinquishing identification with an idealised version of themselves and replacing it with a liberated version capable of living autonomously. Through a composite case, the paper illustrates how these conflicts manifest in the therapeutic setting through transference dynamics. Themes explored include gender dysphoria, confusion, adolescence, and transition.

Rachel Acheson

Rachel Acheson

rachel.acheson117@gmail.com

Rachel Acheson  

Having looked in the last issue of the Research Digest at some of the many studies providing an evidence base for parent-infant psychotherapy, I now turn to an area in which we as a profession are much weaker when it comes to research. ‘Parent work’, as it is termed, is a core skill and essential training requirement for child and adolescent psychotherapists. Depending on the work we go on to do post-qualification, we may find that meetings with parents form a substantive portion of our clinical hours, either in parallel to therapeutic work with children, or as a sole intervention to support a child.

I have often found that this kind of work is not well understood by colleagues from different training backgrounds, who can sometimes view the sole aim of parent work as supporting the child’s engagement in their own therapy. Indeed, there is a large body of research literature in this area, some of which is included in this digest (Alonso & Little, 2019). While narrow in terms of its view of parental role, it also implicitly locates the ‘problem’ within the child, which may be far from the case. However, our colleagues can be forgiven for their lack of appreciation of this way of working, as while I am aware of many theoretical and clinical texts that look in depth at how we can work psychoanalytically with parents (such as ‘Dialogues with Parents’ by Margaret Rustin1, and ‘Core Principles of Assessment and Therapeutic Communication with Children, Parents and Families’ by Ruth Schmidt Neven2) we have been slow to research, and thus evidence, this way of working.

Recent research in the child psychotherapy field has supported an understanding that parallel parent work as essential when a young person is receiving treatment. For example, short term psychoanalytic psychotherapy (STPP) for adolescents with depression that was researched as part of the IMPACT trial, offered seven sessions for parents and carers alongside the 28 offered to the index patient3, and a feasibility trial for treatment-resistant conduct disorder in latency aged children offered the same number of sessions for parents and children separately4. However, although these interventions were found to be effective, the contribution of parent work to the outcome is unclear.

lw433@cam.ac.uk

Lewis Wynn   Director of Studies in Philosophy and College Lecturer in English and Philosophy at Downing College, Cambridge.
Eating disorders, inpatient treatment, multidisciplinary teamwork, anorexia nervosa, CBT, holding environment

This paper attempts to identify and to describe the implicit understanding of mind and mental life at work across an adolescent inpatient eating disorder ward, where the author worked as a healthcare assistant for 12 weeks. It does so by providing an account of ‘prompts’ employed by hospital staff during mealtimes on the ward. The vision of mental illness implied by these ‘prompts’ is described as supporting a paradigm of mental life consistent with the assumptions of cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT). An account of supervising mealtimes while employing language consistent with a psychodynamic model of mind is briefly offered as an alternative, before some of the benefits and drawbacks of both paradigms are outlined.

Nick Midgley   Child and adolescent psychotherapist, and Professor of Psychological Therapies with Children and Young People at UCL/Anna Freud, where he is director of the Child Attachment and Psychological Therapies Research Unit (ChAPTRe). His books include ‘Minding the child: mentalization-based interventions with children, young people and families’ (Routledge, 2012), ‘Time-limited mentalization-based therapy with children (MBT-C): a treatment guide’ (American Psychological Association, 2017) and ‘Therapeutic work for children with complex trauma: a three-track psychodynamic approach’ (Routledge, 2023).
Psychoanalytic psychotherapy, child and adolescent psychotherapy, qualitative methods, meta-synthesis, systematic review

The development of evidence-based practice guidelines for psychotherapy is based primarily on the findings from randomised controlled trials, but there is also a need to understand and learn from the experience of those who attend therapy. Some studies have begun to examine the experience of children and adolescents who have been in psychoanalytic psychotherapy. However, no investigations to date have synthesised this body of work and drawn clinical implications from this research. Therefore, this study aimed to provide the first qualitative meta-synthesis of empirical studies examining children and young people’s experiences of psychoanalytic psychotherapy. Articles meeting the inclusion criteria (n = 11) addressed treatments taking place in the UK, Scandinavia and Western Europe, and most of them focused on those who were in therapy as adolescents. The overall methodological quality of the studies was high. Based on the qualitative meta-synthesis, four over-arching themes were identified: (1) Children and adolescents learn to navigate their role during therapy; (2) The importance of the therapeutic relationship; (3) Psychoanalytic psychotherapy as a ‘painful’ process; and (4) Perceived impact of psychotherapy varies and is difficult to gauge. Some of the findings were consistent with the literature on adults’ experiences of psychoanalytic therapy, as well as young people’s experiences of other types of therapy. However, the findings also point to certain unique features of psychoanalytic psychotherapy for children and adolescents. The clinical implications of the findings are discussed.

Rachel Acheson

Rachel Acheson

rachel.acheson117@gmail.com

Rachel Acheson  

This issue of the Research Digest is taking a closer look at some of the studies that were used in the recent systematic review and meta-analysis of psychodynamic interventions for children under the age of five and their caregivers.1 For those not familiar with it, this review was commissioned by the ACP and conducted by a team at the Anna Freud Centre led by Dr Michelle Sleed. The meta-analysis of controlled studies found significant intervention effects compared to control conditions across a number of domains, including parental reflective functioning, maternal depression, infant behaviour, and infant attachment. In briefer terms – psychodynamic and psychoanalytic ways of working with infants and their carers were shown to be effective.

The ACP launched this review with an online event in October 2022. Becky Saunders (co-lead of the ACP 0–5 supported clinical network) in her introduction emphasised the importance of this piece of research, which she believes will allow child and adolescent psychotherapists to further understand and make the case for our work. This review was commissioned to help inform our contribution to the policy, service and workforce developments taking place across the UK. Whilst the psychoanalytic community have been pioneers in understanding of the importance of early life, and the significance of early childhood development is now widely accepted, she highlighted what she called an ‘implementation gap’. The Nuffield Trust reported in 2021 that more than one in three (36%) children and families with a child under five living in the UK live in poverty,2 and although good quality perinatal mental health services do exist, with less than 40 in the UK, families face a postcode lottery for services. While this may be in part because of austerity government, Becky also reminded us how difficult the messages contained in this kind of work can be to hear, and act upon, and emphasised our responsibility to advocate on behalf of our patients. The findings contained in this review increase our evidence base as a profession and this awareness can embolden us to speak with authority when we contribute to the development of services.

Nataliya Zueva

Nataliya Zueva   Training Child and Adolescent Psychotherapist of the St. Petersburg Society of Child Psychoanalysis, Supervisor. Member of Child and Adolescent Section for RF of the EFPP (European Federation of Psychoanalytic Psychotherapy). Working in private practice with children, adolescents, and families.
Father, fatherhood, loneliness, primary environment, separation anxiety, Oedipus complex

This paper contains thoughts on the journey a man undertakes when he becomes the father to a newborn child, and on the difficulties he faces. Drawing on both psychoanalytic theory and clinical experience the author considers the journey to fatherhood men undertake, exploring the need for them to tolerate change and loneliness as they support and protect the new mother-infant dyad. While infantile anxieties of abandonment may be aroused, the importance of the father’s role in the newly established family is emphasised, particularly in relation to the child finding their own identity. Throughout the paper, parallels are drawn between the role of the father and the role of psychoanalyst or psychotherapist.

Maria Papadima , Catherine Campbell , Nikolaos Tzikas and Fembe Nanji-Rowe

Fembe Nanji-Rowe

Bay Tree House, Christchurch Close, Enfield, EN2 6NZ, UK
maria@mariapapadima.com

Fembe Nanji-Rowe   A child and adolescent psychotherapist in doctoral training at the Independent Psychoanalytic Child and Adolescent Psychotherapy Association (IPCAPA) and trainee member of the Association of Child Psychotherapists (ACP) and British Psychotherapy Foundation (BPF). Fembe is in a full-time clinical placement across Enfield generic CAMHS and Enfield CAMHS Service for Adolescents and Families in Enfield (2022-2026). She has an active interest in cross-cultural phenomena, processes of mourning and the dynamics of race.
Short-term psychodynamic psychotherapy, adolescent crisis intervention, self-harm in adolescents, adolescent psychotherapy, parent-teenager relationships, two therapists working together

The global rise in adolescent self-harm and suicidal behaviours has intensified the demand for mental health services in the UK. This has further strained already underfunded and understaffed resources, resulting in longer waiting times and increased emergency department visits among teenagers. To address the overwhelming need for effective community-based emergency support, a brief psychodynamic crisis therapeutic intervention was developed within a CAMHS adolescent crisis team, inspired by child psychotherapist Ruth Schmidt Neven's work on time-limited psychotherapy with adolescents and their families. This 12-session intervention offers both individual therapy for the adolescent and sessions for their parents, along with regular family reviews. Two psychotherapists work closely together on each case – one with the young person, the other with the parents. The brief model views crises as opportunities for deeper understanding, moving beyond diagnostic and symptom-centred approaches, as well as standard risk management and safety-planning strategies, and underlines the centrality of parent involvement in adolescent crisis work. This paper outlines the intervention's theoretical foundation, guiding principles, and practical design, and presents preliminary findings from a pilot study of 22 cases, run over two and a half years. Early results suggest broad potential for this psychodynamic crisis approach in various adolescent crises, and merit further investigation.

Tami Pollak

Jaffa, Israel

Tami Pollak   Clinical psychotherapist and supervisor in a private clinic and in a day care unit for children with ASD. She teaches on the ‘primitive mental state’ track of the psychotherapy programme at Tel-Aviv University, Israel, and has a PhD in integrating psychoanalytic object-relation metapsychology with French phenomenology. Mrs Pollak has published the article ‘The body-container’ in the International Journal of Psychoanalysis, ‘The body and the consulting room’s materiality as a path for developing inter-subjective psychophysical space’ and ‘Autistic twisted loops’ in the Journal of Child Psychotherapy, and several more articles in Israeli psychoanalytic journals. She has edited the book ‘Treating children with autistic spectrum disorders: a psychoanalytic and developmental approach’ (2017), in which she also contributed two chapters. She is also the author of the book ‘The BodI - psychophysical space as transitional space’ (2018), published in Israel, which is now in the process of being translated to English.
Oedipus complex, early Oedipal organisation, autism, sensorimotor capacities, mental development

The assumption that primal phantasmatic activity stems from bodily functions is widely accepted in developmental and psychoanalytic thinking. This article attempts to give more specific meaning to this abstract assumption. It examines the influence of sensory, perceptual, and motor capacities on the consolidation of typically differentiated erotogenic experiences relevant to pre-Oedipal and Oedipal organisations. It then proceeds to examine the impact of innate deficiencies in these capacities on the development of phantasmatic organisation in children on the autistic spectrum who often manifest atypical erotogenic organisation. Additionally, it pays attention to non-symbolic therapeutic communication and the unconscious transference-countertransference relationship stemming from such a problematic matrix. The paper is clinically derived from a description of the early-Oedipal organisation of a child with low cognitive and functional capacities and proceeds to the manifestations of the Oedipal constellation of a high-functioning autistic child.

This fascinating book, written by Judith Edwards, explores the role, or the potential role, grandmothers can play within a family. This feels highly relevant in today’s world of complex childcare arrangements, multicultural families and stretched family budgets. The book examines the grandparenting position through a number of different lenses, as it explores how precarious and uncertain the role can sometimes be.

In general, the book is written in such a way as to reach a wide audience and is not limited to those professionals who are psychoanalytically trained, concentrating more on the emotional aspects of the relationship than on a psychoanalytic construct. This makes the work a valuable asset for teachers, mothers, aunties, and anyone within the community who wants to be able to reach in and access the richness of ideas that Grandmotherland offers.

Evrinomy Avdi   Professor of Clinical Psychology at the School of Psychology, Aristotle University of Thessaloniki, Greece, and Research Tutor at the Anna Freud, London. She is director of the Laboratory of Applied Psychology, Aristotle University, where she conducts research, works clinically and provides clinical supervision. Her main research interests concern psychotherapy research; she uses qualitative approaches to study therapy process, primarily using discursive, dialogical and narrative analytic methods in conjunction with analysing nonverbal interaction and physiological activation.
Child psychoanalytic psychotherapy, parent work, parental therapy, psychotherapy of parenthood, parent support, concurrent parent work

Born out of the traditional model of psychoanalysis for adults, child psychoanalytic psychotherapists initially focused primarily on their young patients’ inner world. Cultural, economic, and theoretical changes have, however, led child psychotherapists to re-evaluate the importance of the environment, and particularly the role of parents, in the lives of children and young people. In contemporary clinical practice, child psychotherapists often include work with parents when addressing mental health difficulties in children and adolescents. However, no clear theoretical and clinical framework exists for working with parents in psychoanalytic child psychotherapy. This paper provides an overview of the various ways child psychoanalytic psychotherapists engage with parents, as well as a discussion of the commonalities and divergences in different psychoanalytic approaches to parent work. The aim of the paper is to synthesise current literature and to clarify this area of work. This is a narrative review of the literature on the types of engagement and models of work with parents of children and adolescents currently offered by child psychoanalytic psychotherapists. The literature reflects the absence of one accepted formulation and practice in parent work. Despite the growing literature, the lack of cross-referencing and shared language using existing and new psychoanalytic ideas perpetuates the field's fragmentation. In the current cultural and economic context, where other modalities thrive on evidence-based data, the survival of child psychoanalytic psychotherapy in public mental health provision is uncertain. An integrated formulation is needed both to help therapists in their work with parents and allow the evaluation of work with families.

Nikki Eriksen

Nikki Eriksen

Coatbridge, Scotland, UK

Nikki Eriksen   A child and adolescent psychotherapist working in North Lanarkshire CAMHS. She also teaches on the Masters in Therapeutic Work with Children and Young People at Human Development Scotland.
Systematic review, parent work, mental illness, child psychotherapy, research

This literature review adopted a systematic approach to explore and review all of the existing journal literature on parent work in child psychotherapy; studies included span a range of approaches, settings and contexts for this work. Prevalent themes are identified and three main types of journal articles are classified, including an evaluation of the strengths and limitations of their validity as research and/or clinical relevance. Accounts of this work representing diverse parental experiences and exploring direct parental perspectives and opinions of this are identified as a significant gap in the literature. The experiences of parents facing severe and enduring mental health challenges in particular are found to be under-represented, and the case is made for more research in this area. The review was conducted to inform a research project undertaken by the author within their clinical training placement, which became the first of the new professional Doctorates completed at Human Development Scotland; some reflections are included about the challenge of undertaking a literature review of such broad scope while both child psychotherapy trainee and novice trainee researcher.
